explanations.answer: They have been born of God and know God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The writer says, “Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.” Love comes from God, and the ones who love carry His family name. Born, not hired. Nobody fills out an application for that.

explanations.answer: They have earned a place with God
explanations.explanation: Close to how a lot of us think, but that's not what the text says. It says everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Being born into a family is not a paycheck, and no timecard gets punched for it. I think that's good news for anybody tired of keeping score.

explanations.answer: They have been chosen to lead others
explanations.explanation: I get why that one looks tempting, friend, it sounds official. But the writer never says anything about leading. He says everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. No clipboard, no title, no fancy name tag.

Not this time, friend. Verse 8 says, “Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.” So the writer ties knowing God and loving together. Somebody who doesn't love isn't doing fine on the knowing side.
Yes, friend, False. The writer says, “Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.” He doesn't leave a loophole in there. Knowing God and loving go together in this letter.

explanations.answer: He sent His one and only Son into the world
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. God's love was revealed when He sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. The writer points to a Person, not a program. Love showed up with a name and an address.

explanations.answer: He sent a prophet into every single nation
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the writer doesn't say that. He says God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. A prophet is a messenger, and this is bigger than a messenger. I think "one and only" is the part to hang onto.

explanations.answer: He wrote His law on two tablets of stone
explanations.explanation: That happened, friend, but it's not what this verse points to. Moses, Israel's leader, received two tablets of stone from God (Exodus 31:18). Here the writer says God's love was revealed when He sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him.

explanations.answer: Not that we loved God but that He loved us
explanations.explanation: Baked into the verse, friend. “…not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” Love starts on His side, not ours. We're catching up, not leading the way.

explanations.answer: Not that we obeyed God but that we kept trying
explanations.explanation: Hang on, friend, that one flips the direction. The writer says love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us. Nothing in the verse puts the starting point on our effort. It's all about what He did first.

explanations.answer: Not that we feared God but that we served Him
explanations.explanation: That one points the wrong way, friend, because it's still about us. The verse says love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. The writer keeps his eyes on what God did. Even later he says, “We love because He first loved us.”
Yes, friend, sins. God sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. That's what He did, and the writer says it plainly. I think that plain talk is a gift.

I see why fears came to mind, since the letter talks about fear later on. But this verse says God sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. The word is sins. Fear gets its own turn in verse 18.

Doubts is a natural guess, friend, we've all got a few lying around. But the text says God sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. That's the word the writer chose, and it's the one that fits.

explanations.answer: God remains in us and His love is perfected in us
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. No one has ever seen God, but the writer says that if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us. We can't see Him, yet love among us shows He's near. That's a mighty big result from a small act.

explanations.answer: We will see God face to face in this life
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text, friend. The writer says, “No one has ever seen God.” What he promises is that if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us.

explanations.answer: We will never again be tempted to sin
explanations.explanation: That's a big promise, but the verse doesn't make it. It says that if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us. Nothing in it speaks of temptation. I'd rather stick to what the writer actually gave us.

explanations.answer: He has given us of His Spirit
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The writer says, “By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit.” The proof isn't something we produce, it's something He gave. And a gift is a lot easier to hold onto than a résumé.

explanations.answer: We have never once doubted Him
explanations.explanation: Whew, if that were the test, friend, I'd be in trouble. The writer doesn't say that. He says we know we remain in Him, and He in us, because He has given us of His Spirit. The proof is what He gave.

explanations.answer: We have done many good works
explanations.explanation: Good works sound like a fair guess, but that's not the reason given here. The writer says we know we remain in Him, and He in us, because He has given us of His Spirit. It's about what He gave, not about a tally of what we did.
True, friend. The verse says, “If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.” Notice the word anyone. The writer keeps it open to whoever confesses.

It's True, friend, though I can see why you might hesitate. Verse 15 says, “If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.” That's exactly what the writer says. Anyone who confesses it is in.
Love is the word, friend. “God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” To abide means to stay put, to make a home. And here the home is love.

Truth is a good word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The writer says, “God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” The word that gets repeated is love. He even says it twice in the same breath.

Peace is a lovely thing to want, friend, but this verse doesn't use it. It says, “God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” So the blank is love. The letter keeps coming back to that one word.
Confidence, yes, friend. Love is perfected among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment. Not dread, not nerves. The writer says confidence.

I get it, friend, a big day like that can make a person's knees knock. But the writer says love is perfected among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment. Dread isn't the word he picked. He picked confidence.

Excuses, friend? I've got a whole stack of those for the oven when a batch runs late. But the writer says love is perfected among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment. He doesn't hand us excuses, he hands us confidence.

explanations.answer: In this world we are just like Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives, friend. The writer says, “…for in this world we are just like Him.” The confidence comes from being like Him, not from a spotless record. That's all the verse says, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: In this world we have done no wrong
explanations.explanation: That's a bold claim, friend, and the writer never makes it. The reason he gives is, “…for in this world we are just like Him.” The confidence rests on being like Him, not on a perfect record.

explanations.answer: In this world we have kept His law
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, but it's not what the verse says. The writer gives this reason: “…for in this world we are just like Him.” No law-keeping tally shows up here. The reason is about being like Him.
Yep, friend. “…perfect love drives out fear…” Driven out, like a squatter getting the boot. When perfect love moves in, fear doesn't get a vote.
Courage is a nice word, friend, but the writer doesn't use it here. He says, “…perfect love drives out fear…” Fear doesn't get converted into something. It gets driven out.
A trade sounds neighborly, but that's not how the verse puts it. The writer says, “…perfect love drives out fear…” Nothing swaps places with it. Fear is driven out.

True, friend. The writer gives the reason right there: “…because fear involves punishment.” He doesn't go on to explain more, so I won't either. He says there is no fear in love, and that's the reason he gives.

It's True, friend, so no need to fret. The writer says, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment.” That's the reason he gives for why perfect love drives out fear.

Yes, a liar. The writer doesn't tiptoe, friend: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar.” That's a strong word. He's looking at what a person says next to how that person treats his brother.
A beginner sounds gentle, friend, but that's not the word he uses. The writer says, “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar.” He doesn't soften it. The word is liar.
Stranger is a softer word than the one he picked. The writer says, “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar.” He uses a plain, strong word and doesn't dress it up. Liar.
Not so, friend. The writer says, “For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.” He says cannot. So the answer is False.

False is right, friend. The writer says, “For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.” The brother you can see, and the God you can't. And the writer says one doesn't go without the other.
That's the one, friend. “And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well.” It comes straight from Him. It's a commandment, not a suggestion.

Close on the tone, but the source is off. The writer says, “And we have this commandment from Him…” That's from Him, not from a custom. The commandment is that whoever loves God must love his brother as well.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, is known for his sayings, so I see the pull. But this letter doesn't mention him here. The writer says, “And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well.” It's a commandment from Him.
